title: What qualifications and first aid training do early childhood educators need in Australia?
description: Educator qualification rules in the Education and Care Services National Regulations: regulation 126, early childhood teachers and regulation 136 first aid.
shortAnswer: Under the Education and Care Services National Regulations, at least 50% of educators counted in ratios at a centre-based service for children preschool age or under must hold, or be actively working towards, an approved diploma, and the rest an approved certificate III. Services must also engage or have access to early childhood teachers by attendance numbers, and regulation 136 requires current approved first aid, anaphylaxis and emergency asthma management training.
keyTakeaways: Regulation 126 sets the 50% diploma and certificate III rule for educators counted toward ratios in centre-based services for children preschool age or under.
Only qualifications on the approved list kept by the Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority (ACECQA), or ones ACECQA assesses as equivalent, count.
Early childhood teacher (ECT) requirements scale with attendance: 20% access below 25 children, an ECT in attendance from 25, and a second ECT or suitably qualified person from 60.
Since the regulation changes from October 1, 2023, first aid, anaphylaxis and asthma training are current for three years, but CPR and emergency life support only for one year.
Regulation 242 (taken to be an ECT while studying) and the remote area ECT provisions are scheduled to expire on December 31, 2026 where they still apply.
jurisdiction: Australia (national: Education and Care Services National Law and National Regulations, applied in each state and territory)
regulator: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority (ACECQA), with state and territory regulatory authorities such as the NSW Early Learning Commission
appliesTo: Approved providers and nominated supervisors of long day care, preschool and kindergarten services regulated under the National Quality Framework
Educators counted toward educator to child ratios in centre-based services for children preschool age or under
Family day care educators and family day care co-ordinators
Registered training organizations and higher education providers seeking ACECQA approval of education and care or first aid courses

sections.heading: What do the National Regulations require of educator qualifications?

blocks.text: The Education and Care Services National Regulations require minimum qualification levels for every educator counted in educator to child ratios, not just for leaders. ACECQA's [qualification requirements for centre-based services](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/qualifications/requirements/children-preschool-age-or-under) state that under regulation 126, 50% of the educators required to meet ratios in a centre-based service with children preschool age and under "must have, or be actively working towards, an approved diploma level education and care qualification (or higher)".

All other educators counted in ratios must hold, or be actively working towards, at least an approved certificate III level education and care qualification. The National Quality Framework (NQF) treats a person as diploma or certificate III qualified if they hold an approved qualification at that level, hold a former approved qualification completed before January 1, 2012, or hold a qualification ACECQA has assessed as equivalent.

The Regulations set levels, not duties. ACECQA notes that the National Regulations "do not specify what roles or responsibilities a diploma level educator must undertake"; that is a decision for the approved provider. For a training manager, the regulatory question is therefore binary per person (approved qualification at the right level, or a documented and current study enrollment), while role scope sits in the provider's own [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the National Regulations as described by ACECQA and the NSW Department of Education as at November 2026. Several transitional provisions end on December 31, 2026. Western Australia applies its own version of the National Law and Regulations and some commencement dates differ there.

sections.heading: When can an educator count while still studying?

blocks.text: An educator who is "actively working towards" an approved qualification may be counted at that level, under regulations 126(1) and 127, with the term defined in regulation 10. According to ACECQA's [actively working towards guidance](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/qualifications/requirements/actively-working-towards-a-qualification), the person must be enrolled in an ACECQA approved qualification and have started study, be making satisfactory progress, and be meeting the requirements to maintain enrollment.

items: **Certificate III level:** enrolled, started, progressing and maintaining enrollment.
**Diploma level:** the same conditions, plus either holding an approved certificate III or having completed 30% of the units in an approved ECT qualification.

**Taken to be an ECT (regulation 242):** enrolled in an approved ECT qualification, with documentary evidence from the course provider, and holding an approved diploma or having completed at least 50% of the course. Regulation 242 does not apply in Queensland or Victoria, or in NSW centre-based services with 30 or more children preschool age or under.

**Family day care:** from July 1, 2023, new family day care educators must hold an approved certificate III before starting and cannot rely on actively working towards. Family day care co-ordinators must hold an approved diploma and cannot rely on it either.

blocks.text: Education Ministers agreed to extend regulation 242 in the ACT, NSW, NT, SA, Tasmania and WA to December 31, 2026. After that date an educator must have completed the ECT qualification to count as an ECT, although ACECQA notes they may still count as a diploma educator or suitably qualified person depending on how much of the degree they have completed.

sections.heading: How many early childhood teachers does a service need?

blocks.text: The number of early childhood teachers depends on how many children preschool age or under are in attendance at any one time, under regulations 129 to 135, with NSW specific requirements in regulation 272. The [Guide to the NQF, Quality Area 4](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/national-quality-framework/guide-nqf/section-4-operational-requirements/quality-area-4-staffing-arrangements) and ACECQA's qualification page set out the tiers below.

blocks.text: A suitably qualified person is someone actively working towards an approved ECT qualification who has completed at least 50% of it or holds an approved diploma, or a registered (in NSW, accredited) primary or secondary teacher who also holds an ACECQA approved diploma or higher. Teacher registration is not an NQF requirement for ECTs, but some state and territory laws require it.

A transitional provision in regulation 239A lets remote and very remote services in NSW, the Northern Territory, South Australia, Tasmania and Western Australia meet attendance rules through access to an ECT for set percentages of time. The Guide states that this provision "is scheduled to expire" in those jurisdictions on December 31, 2026, so remote providers should plan recruitment or study pathways now.

sections.heading: What first aid, anaphylaxis and asthma training does regulation 136 require?

blocks.text: Regulation 136 requires centre-based and family day care services to have educators with current approved first aid qualifications, anaphylaxis management training and emergency asthma management training. The NSW Department of Education's [first aid resource page](https://education.nsw.gov.au/early-childhood-education/ecec-resource-library/first-aid-cpr-kids) describes regulation 136 in exactly those terms and warns that general awareness videos do not satisfy it: only qualifications and training approved by ACECQA count.

Currency is now written into the Regulations. ACECQA's [first aid qualifications page](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/qualifications/requirements/first-aid-qualifications-training) states that from October 1, 2023, the following are taken to be current only if attained or undertaken within the previous three years: approved first aid qualifications, approved anaphylaxis management training, and approved emergency asthma management training. The exception is emergency life support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) training, which "must be completed within the previous year to be taken as current".

Providers had until April 1, 2024 to bring existing staff into line, which ACECQA's [2023 regulation change notice](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/latest-news/blog/regulation-changes-family-day-care-educator-qualifications-and-first-aid-currency-periods) describes as the commencement of the three year currency period, with the WA timing noted separately. ACECQA adds that currency applies to each individual unit of competency on a certificate, so a single certificate can contain units that expire on different dates.

Course providers apply to ACECQA to have first aid, emergency asthma management and anaphylaxis management courses added to the approved NQF qualifications list. ACECQA's [course approval page](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/qualifications/assessment/approval/first-aid-and-training) states that nationally accredited courses are approved for five years and non-accredited courses typically for three, with the option of extension to five.

blocks.text: Each NQF qualification obligation attaches to a defined role and produces a record an authorized officer can ask to see. The table below is an original mapping drawn from the regulations cited by ACECQA; it is a planning aid, not a substitute for the Regulations.

blocks.text: Two features of this table matter for [audit preparation](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit). First, the qualification test is applied against the roster, so the evidence must show who was counted in ratios at a given time, not just who is employed. Second, first aid currency expires unit by unit, which makes a single renewal date per person unreliable; tracking it is a [refresh cycle](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) problem rather than an onboarding one.

Staff records are the primary evidence. The Guide to the NQF states that authorized officers may ask to see the record of educators working directly with children in centre-based services, or the record of staff, family day care educators, co-ordinators and assistants in family day care, required under regulations 153 and 177. Those records "should include evidence of any relevant qualification held by the staff members", or evidence such as a transcript or letter from the course provider for someone actively working towards one.

Where a primary school teacher covers a certificate III or diploma educator under regulation 126A, regulation 152A requires the approved provider to record the full name of the person replaced, the role, the replacement's qualification, the dates and the reason for absence. Each role can be replaced for no more than 30 days in total in the 12 months before the day of replacement, pro rata for part time roles.

Qualification records also connect to child safety obligations that commenced in 2026, including the National Early Childhood Worker Register. Those training duties are covered separately in [child protection and child safety training for NSW early childhood services](/regulations/child-protection-training-early-childhood-nsw), and screening is covered in [working with children check requirements](/regulations/working-with-children-check-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each NQF obligation as a structured requirement tied to a role, an approved qualification or unit of competency, and an expiry rule, so currency gaps surface before a roster is affected. Evidence such as certificates and enrollment letters is linked to the requirement it satisfies, which keeps the record usable when an authorized officer asks for it.

faqs.q: Does regulation 126 apply to outside school hours care?
faqs.a: No. ACECQA's Guide to the NQF states there are no national qualification requirements for educators at centre-based services educating and caring for children over preschool age. The ACT, Queensland, South Australia, Victoria and Western Australia set their own requirements for those services, so outside school hours care providers need to check the rules of their state or territory regulatory authority.

faqs.q: Is a first aid certificate from any provider acceptable?
faqs.a: Only qualifications and training on ACECQA's approved list satisfy regulation 136. The NSW Department of Education states that non-approved learning, such as its own first aid video, does not meet the requirement. Course providers must apply to ACECQA for approval, and approved courses are listed on the approved NQF qualifications list.

Yes, if ACECQA assesses it as equivalent to an approved certificate III, diploma or early childhood teaching qualification. ACECQA's qualification pages list ACECQA equivalence assessment as one of the ways a person is treated as qualified at each level, alongside holding a current or former approved qualification.

faqs.q: What happens to student ECTs after December 31, 2026?
faqs.a: Regulation 242 has been extended in the ACT, NSW, NT, SA, Tasmania and WA only to December 31, 2026. After it expires, ACECQA says an educator needs to have completed the ECT qualification to be considered a qualified ECT, although they may still count as a diploma level educator or suitably qualified person depending on progress.
